1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
5	\label{sec:discuss_kstar}
6	
7	The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
8	Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations and 4 decoding strategies; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.
9	
10	The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
11	The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
12	At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions; Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}, Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; see also Figure~\ref{fig:s1_auc_decay_ci} in the Appendix), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
13	By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917 across all eight model$\times$decoding conditions (upper bound from nucleus $p{=}0.9$ decoding; Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay})---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
14	Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.
15	
16	The feature degradation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides mechanistic evidence for this rapid collapse.
17	The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
18	Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
19	The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
20	Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs; Table~\ref{tab:top_features}), suggesting that the two-step information loss is driven primarily by the autoregressive generation mechanism rather than by model-specific biases at this scale.
21	
22	This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
23	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
24	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
25	Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
26	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.
27	
28	Importantly, $\Kempirical = 2$ is an \emph{operational} lower bound conditioned on the 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set; the \emph{theoretical} boundary $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.
29	Preliminary evidence from a neural probing experiment supports this distinction.
30	A frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder (1536-dimensional last-layer representations) paired with a lightweight MLP classifier (Table~\ref{tab:s7_neural_probe}) achieves 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$) on the Qwen-continuation dataset, exceeding the $\theta = 0.60$ threshold that the same dataset's LightGBM classifier fails to cross ($\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
31	This yields $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$: the learned representation recovers one additional discriminable boundary that the hand-crafted features miss.
32	The improvement is concentrated at the 2v3 pair ($+$5.86\,pp over LightGBM); at the already-separable 1v2 boundary the neural probe achieves 0.6983 versus 0.6112, a substantial gain but one that does not alter the boundary determination.
33	At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any hand-crafted configuration---suggesting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.
34	The lossy-channel narrative remains intact: even with 1536-dimensional frozen representations, the discrimination boundary extends to only three steps, confirming that the information bottleneck of recursive generation is shallow even with substantially richer representations.
35	These results are preliminary: they cover a single model-dataset pair (Qwen-continuation) and lack bootstrap confidence intervals; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.
36	
37	The consistency of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
38	Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay}; Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
39	Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
40	This robustness suggests that, at least at the $\leq$1.5B scale, $\Kempirical$ is governed primarily by the information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.
41	
42	\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
43	\label{sec:discuss_transfer}
44	
45	The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
46	Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs (Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix}; see Table~\ref{tab:s1_transfer} for the full matrix).
47	At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 across all tested model pairs, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across the tested generators.
48	
49	The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
50	This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.
51	
52	Two caveats bound this conclusion.
53	First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
54	The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
55	Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.
56	
57	\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
58	\label{sec:discuss_features}
59

Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.

\emph{Decoding coverage.}
We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
$\Kempirical \geq 2$ across $\theta \in \{0.55, 0.60, 0.65\}$ for all four decoding strategies, rising to $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$ (all four 2v3 $\auc$ values exceed 0.55) and returning to $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\theta \in \{0.60, 0.65\}$.
At $\theta = 0.70$, three of four decoding configurations collapse to $\Kempirical = 1$; only the high-temperature setting ($T{=}1.2$) retains $\Kempirical = 2$, consistent with its elevated 1v2 $\auc$ (0.7039).
Beyond decoding parameters, the threshold sensitivity extends to generation mode: at $\theta{=}0.70$, $\Kempirical{=}1$ for all four model-mode configurations; at $\theta{=}0.65$, continuation-mode configurations already drop to $\Kempirical{=}1$, while rewrite mode retains $\Kempirical{=}2$.
Our current analysis primarily covers the decoding configuration axis.
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary---as the neural probe results confirm, where a richer representation pushes the 2v3 pair above $\theta$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}).
Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.

\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.
Preliminary neural probing results provide direct evidence for this gap: on the Qwen-continuation dataset, a frozen-encoder MLP achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$) compared to $\Kempirical = 2$ with 15-dimensional hand-crafted features (2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
This confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal and that $\Ktheory \geq 3$.
However, the neural probe result rests on a single dataset and awaits cross-model validation and bootstrap confidence intervals before a firm revision of the headline $\Kempirical$ can be claimed.

\emph{Feature representation.}
The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is not optimal.
A preliminary neural probing experiment demonstrates that frozen LLM embeddings (1536 dimensions) paired with a lightweight MLP push $\Kempirical$ from~2 to~3 on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}), confirming that learned representations capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss.
The magnitude of the gain---2v3 $\auc$ rising from 0.5609 to 0.6195---indicates meaningful recoverable signal beyond what hand-crafted features extract.
Full characterization of this gap, including cross-model generalization and bootstrap uncertainty quantification, remains future work.

\paragraph{Graduated Filtering.}
Results for graduated filtering will be added upon completion of ongoing experiments.

\subsection{Broader Impact}
\label{sec:broader_impact}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.

\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.

\paragraph{$\Kstar$ as a corpus audit metric.}
Independent of filtering applications, $\Kstar$ provides an actionable corpus quality metric answering a concrete question: what fraction of a training corpus consists of depth-$\geq 2$ synthetic text?
Since $\Kempirical = 2$ implies that texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are statistically indistinguishable from depth-1 text, they should be treated equivalently in data curation.
This establishes a directly actionable threshold: texts exceeding $\Kstar$ generations require no finer-grained depth discrimination and can be assigned to a single ``deep synthetic'' category, simplifying dataset audits even when the efficacy of graduated filtering remains to be established.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.

\paragraph{AI text detection.}
Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.
This additional dimension---how many generations of processing a text has undergone---may prove valuable for provenance tracking and corpus quality assessment, where the binary human/AI label elides important distinctions between lightly and heavily recycled content.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
5	Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
6	All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
7	Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
8	We organize results around four questions:
9	(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
10	(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
11	(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
12	(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?
13	
14	%% ====================================================================
15	\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
16	\label{sec:kstar_boundary}
17	
18	Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
19	across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
20	(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
21	and 2v3 boundaries.
22	
23	\begin{table}[t]
24	\centering
25	\small
26	\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
27	and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
28	2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
29	and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
30	All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
31	\label{tab:kstar_ci}

34	 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
35	\midrule
36	0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]

62	\end{tabular}
63	\end{table}
64	
65	The pattern is consistent across all four configurations:
66	0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
67	followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
68	with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
69	($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
70	All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
71	Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.
72	
73	\begin{figure}[t]
74	\centering
75	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
76	\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
77	\label{fig:auc_decay}
78	\end{figure}
79	
80	For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
81	$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
82	OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
83	Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
84	Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
85	Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
86	Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
87	Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at the $\leq$1.5B scale.
88	
89	The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
90	(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
91	indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
92	generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
93	boundary closer to the detection threshold.
94	
95	The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
96	Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
97	Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
98	(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
99	across models in the same mode
100	(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
101	suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
102	of detectability than model identity.
103	We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
104	and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.
105	
106	Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
107	rapidly.
108	OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
109	($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
110	classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
111	random for this model.
112	Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
113	($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
114	while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
115	3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).
116	
117	%% ====================================================================
118	\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
119	\label{sec:transfer}
120	
121	Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
122	To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
123	Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
124	$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
125	classification.
126	
127	\begin{table}[t]
128	\centering
129	\small
130	\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
131	classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
132	Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
133	off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
134	model.}
135	\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
136	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
137	\toprule
138	Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
139	  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
140	\midrule
141	Qwen-rw

143	Pythia

147	Qwen-cont
148	  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
149	\bottomrule
150	\end{tabular}
151	\end{table}
152	
153	\begin{figure}[t]
154	\centering
155	\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
156	\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
157	Rows: training model; columns: test model.
158	Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
159	mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
160	transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
161	Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
162	\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
163	\end{figure}
164	
165	Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
166	First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
167	Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
168	(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
169	The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
170	$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
171	classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
172	predictions is largely preserved.
173	Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
174	(84--85\% accuracy retention),
175	and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
176	These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.
177	
178	Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
179	Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
180	within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
181	(45--50\% by $\tau$).
182	The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
183	This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
184	artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
185	to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.
186	
187	At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
188	for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
189	distinction is consistently transferable across all tested generators
190	and modes.
191	The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
192	(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.
193	
194	The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
195	mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
196	cross-model.
197	This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
198	continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
199	further.
200	
201	%% ====================================================================
202	\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
203	\label{sec:feature_degradation}
204	
205	The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
206	We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
207	We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
208	independently for each model and comparing them via rank
209	correlation.
210	
211	\begin{table}[t]
212	\centering
213	\small
214	\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
215	model configuration.
216	Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
217	Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
218	Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,

377	
378	\paragraph{Interpretation: $\Kstar$ hierarchy.}
379	These preliminary results motivate a three-level hierarchy of discrimination boundaries:
380	\[
381	  \Ktheory \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{15D}}
382	\]
383	where $\Kempirical^{\text{15D}} = 2$ is the operationally deployable boundary measured with model-free, interpretable features, and $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ is a representation-dependent ceiling accessible only through model-specific probing.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}

 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\

The pattern is consistent across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at the $\leq$1.5B scale.

The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.
OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.

$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.

(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).

artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is consistently transferable across all tested generators
and modes.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

\subsection{Representation Dependence of $\Kempirical$}
\label{sec:neural_probe}

The preceding sections establish $\Kempirical = 2$ using a 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set.
A natural question is whether this boundary reflects a fundamental limit of the generational depth signal or an information bottleneck imposed by projecting high-dimensional text representations into 15 statistical summaries.
To disentangle these possibilities, we replace the hand-crafted features with frozen LLM hidden states and train a lightweight MLP probe on the same classification task.

\paragraph{Setup.}
We extract last-layer hidden states from a frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B model (\texttt{float16}), apply attention-masked average pooling to obtain 1536-dimensional document embeddings, and train a two-hidden-layer MLP ($1536 \to 512 \to 256 \to 6$, ReLU, dropout 0.1) with 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Table~\ref{tab:s7_neural_probe}).
The probe's limited capacity ensures that any discriminability reflects depth information already encoded in the frozen representations rather than patterns learned de novo.

\end{tabular}

\paragraph{Interpretation: $\Kstar$ hierarchy.}
These preliminary results motivate a three-level hierarchy of discrimination boundaries:
\[
  \Ktheory \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{neural}} \;\geq\; \Kempirical^{\text{15D}}
\]
where $\Kempirical^{\text{15D}} = 2$ is the operationally deployable boundary measured with model-free, interpretable features, and $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ is a representation-dependent ceiling accessible only through model-specific probing.
The gap between the two confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal: at least one additional discriminable generation boundary exists in the frozen representations but is lost during projection into the hand-crafted feature space.
The theoretical upper bound $\Ktheory$---the boundary achievable with an optimal representation and classifier---remains unknown but is at least~3.

The two $\Kempirical$ estimates serve complementary purposes.
The 15D boundary ($\Kempirical = 2$) is model-free, interpretable, and computationally lightweight: features are extracted from surface-level token statistics without access to model internals, and the LightGBM classifier trains in seconds.
This makes it suitable for deployment in data curation pipelines.
The neural boundary ($\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$) requires a frozen copy of a specific LLM for embedding extraction, is opaque in the features it exploits, and incurs $100\times$+ computational overhead for inference.
It is valuable as a theoretical exploration tool---demonstrating that deeper depth signals \emph{exist}---but impractical for the model-agnostic deployment scenarios where depth estimation is most needed.
Notably, the neural probe's advantage does not alter the headline result for practitioners: $\Kempirical = 2$ remains the relevant boundary for deployable depth estimation with current feature technology.

The 2v3 boundary under neural probing is marginal: the mean $\auc$ of 0.6195 exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$1.95\,pp, and individual fold variation (std $= 0.0094$) places this margin within approximately two standard deviations of the threshold.
These results should be treated as preliminary evidence that the 15D boundary is representation-dependent, not as a firm revision of $\Kempirical$.
